nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the folk novel, the anthropology of the Black South and the woman's voice
literary_identity: Novelist, folklorist and anthropologist; the great recorder of Black Southern folk culture and the author of Their Eyes Were Watching God, the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance.
biography: Born in Notasulga, Alabama, on 7 January 1891 and raised in Eatonville, Florida, the first incorporated Black town in America; she worked as a maid, a waitress and a manicurist, studied at Howard and at Barnard under Franz Boas, and did fieldwork in Florida, New Orleans and Haiti. Jonah's Gourd Vine (1934), Mules and Men (1935), Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), Tell My Horse (1938) and Moses, Man of the Mountain (1939) followed; she died in poverty at Fort Pierce, Florida, on 28 January 1960, and her work was recovered by Alice Walker in the 1970s.
literary_profile: Hurston wrote the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance and the great record of Black Southern folk culture: Their Eyes Were Watching God made a Black woman's voice and a Black woman's desire the centre of an American novel, and Mules and Men preserved a body of folklore that would otherwise have been lost. Her prose — the free indirect rendering of Eatonville speech — is one of the period's great achievements.
stylistic_characteristics: Free indirect style that renders Black Southern speech without condescension; the frame of the tale-teller and the 'lying' session; the folk idiom transcribed as literature; the metaphor drawn from the natural world; the novel structured by a woman's marriages.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the Black South and the folk community; the Black woman's desire and self-making; marriage, work and independence; the Eatonville town and its 'lying' culture; the hurricane, nature and God; the migration north and the return south.
historical_significance: Hurston wrote the finest African American novel of the period and the greatest record of Black Southern folklore: Their Eyes Were Watching God is a permanent American novel, Mules and Men preserved a whole oral culture, and her recovery in the 1970s made her the central woman writer of the Harlem Renaissance.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Jamaican-American; the protest sonnet, the Jamaican dialect poem and the novel of Black labour
literary_identity: Poet and novelist; the first major poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the author of 'If We Must Die' and Home to Harlem.
biography: Born Festus Claudius McKay in Clarendon Parish, Jamaica, on 15 September 1889; he was apprenticed to a wheelwright and then served in the Jamaican constabulary, published Songs of Jamaica and Constab Ballads in 1912, and came to the United States to study at Tuskegee and Kansas State. He moved to Harlem in 1914, published 'If We Must Die' in 1919, Harlem Shadows in 1922, and the novels Home to Harlem (1928), Banjo (1929) and Banana Bottom (1933); he travelled to Russia and France, became a Catholic, and died in Chicago on 22 May 1948.
literary_profile: McKay is the first major poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the author of the period's most famous protest poem: 'If We Must Die' — written during the Red Summer of 1919 and quoted by Churchill in 1940 — gave the movement its trumpet call, Harlem Shadows its first substantial book of verse, and Home to Harlem the first best-selling Black novel of the decade. His Jamaican dialect poems are the first body of West Indian verse in English.
stylistic_characteristics: The sonnet and the ballad used for protest; the Jamaican dialect written phonetically; the blunt, direct, unornamented statement; the image of the body under threat; the travel narrative of the Black migrant worker.
intellectual_concerns: Race and the colour line; the Black worker and the colonial inheritance; the Jamaican folk and the peasantry; Harlem, the cabaret and the migrant's city; the body, desire and the police; the revolutionary and the exile.
historical_significance: McKay wrote the period's most famous protest poem and the first substantial body of verse of the Harlem Renaissance: 'If We Must Die' became an international anthem of resistance, Harlem Shadows gave the movement its first book, and his Jamaican dialect poems founded West Indian literature in English.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Songs of Jamaica (1912); Constab Ballads (1912); Spring in New Hampshire (1920); Harlem Shadows (1922); Home to Harlem (1928, novel); Banjo: A Story Without a Plot (1929, novel); Gingertown (1932, stories); Banana Bottom (1933, novel); A Long Way from Home (1937, autobiography); Harlem: Negro Metropolis (1940, history); Selected Poems of Claude McKay (1953, posthumous); My Green Hills of Jamaica (1979, posthumous); 'If We Must Die' (1919); 'America' (1921); 'The Lynching' (1922); 'Tropics in New York' (1920); 'The Harlem Dancer' (1917); 'Flame-Heart' (1920).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the lyric in the English tradition and the poetry of the colour line
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and anthologist; the most formally accomplished poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the movement's principal defender of the inherited English lyric.
biography: Born Countee LeRoy Porter in New York on 30 May 1903 and raised in Harlem by the Reverend Frederick Asbury Cullen; he won prizes at high school and at New York University, published Color in 1925, graduated from Harvard in 1926, and edited Caroling Dusk (1927), the anthology of Black verse. He married Yolande Du Bois in 1928, taught in the New York schools, and published Copper Sun (1927), The Black Christ (1929), One Way to Heaven (1932) and The Medea and Some Poems (1935). He died in New York on 9 January 1946.
literary_profile: Cullen is the most formally gifted poet of the Harlem Renaissance: Color and Copper Sun contain the finest English lyrics written by an African American of the period, and 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage' and 'Incident' are permanent poems of the colour line. His editorship of Caroling Dusk gave the movement its anthology, and his insistence that a Black poet might use the whole English tradition was the counter-position to Hughes's folk programme.
stylistic_characteristics: The strict English lyric — the sonnet, the ballad, the quatrain and the rhymed octave; the Keatsian and Housmanesque diction; the irony of a formal grace turned on a brutal subject; the refrain and the clanging rhyme; the poem that ends on a question.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line and the burden of a 'double consciousness'; Africa and the ancestral inheritance; the lynch mob and the murdered child; the Christian faith and the Black church; love and the private life; the poet's quarrel with his own tradition.
historical_significance: Cullen is the most formally accomplished poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the author of some of its finest lyrics: Color and Copper Sun are permanent books of American verse, 'Yet Do I Marvel' and 'Heritage' are central poems of the colour line, and Caroling Dusk is the movement's defining anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Color (1925); The Ballad of the Brown Girl (1927); Copper Sun (1927); Caroling Dusk (1927, ed., anthology); The Black Christ and Other Poems (1929); One Way to Heaven (1932, novel); The Medea and Some Poems (1935, translation); The Lost Zoo (1940, children's verse); My Lives and How I Lost Them (1942, children's prose); On These I Stand (1947, posthumous); The Poetry of Countee Cullen (1947, posthumous); 'Yet Do I Marvel' (1925); 'Heritage' (1925); 'Incident' (1925); 'From the Dark Tower' (1925); 'Tableau' (1925); 'Saturday's Child' (1925).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the modernist collage of the Black South and the lyric of passing
literary_identity: Poet and novelist; the author of Cane, the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American modernist texts.
biography: Born Nathan Pinchback Toomer in Washington, D.C., on 26 December 1894, the grandson of a Reconstruction governor of Louisiana and the great-grandson of a slave; he studied at the University of Wisconsin, the Massachusetts College of Agriculture, the American Physical Training College, the University of Chicago and the City College of New York without taking a degree, and taught for a term at a Black school in Sparta, Georgia, in 1921. Cane appeared in 1923; he later joined the Gurdjieff movement, wrote largely unpublished work, became a Quaker, and died at Doylestown, Pennsylvania, on 30 January 1967.
literary_profile: Toomer wrote the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance: Cane — a collage of stories, poems and a play, moving from the Black South to the urban North — is one of the great modernist texts in American literature, and its lyric prose anticipates both Faulkner and Hurston. It is the only major book of the movement that refuses the novel's form altogether.
stylistic_characteristics: The collage of genres (story, poem, drama) in a single book; the lyric prose-poem with a refrain; the crescent-shaped page and the modernist typography; the abrupt shift from the Southern field to the Northern street; the image that returns across the book.
intellectual_concerns: The Black South and the Georgia cane field; the migration north and the urban crowd; race, passing and mixed descent; the woman as a figure of the land; the loss of the folk world; the artist's separation from his own people.
historical_significance: Toomer wrote the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American modernist texts: Cane invented a collage form that American fiction is still absorbing, its lyric prose changed the sound of Black American writing, and it is the only major book of the movement that is formally as advanced as Ulysses or The Waste Land.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Cane (1923); Essentials (1931, Gurdjieff essays); The Flavor of Man (1949, lecture); The Wayward and the Seeking (1980, posthumous); The Collected Poems of Jean Toomer (1988, posthumous); A Drama of the Southwest (2016, posthumous play); The Letters of Jean Toomer (2006, posthumous); 'Karintha' (1923); 'Fern' (1923); 'Blood-Burning Moon' (1923); 'Theater' (1923); 'Bona and Paul' (1923); 'Kabnis' (1923, drama).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the jazz-age novel, the lyric of the American dream and the short story of the twenties
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the laureate of the Jazz Age and the author of The Great Gatsby, the most perfect American novel of the period.
biography: Born Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald in Saint Paul, Minnesota, on 24 September 1896; he read at Princeton without graduating, served in the army without seeing action, and made his name with This Side of Paradise in 1920, marrying Zelda Sayre a week after publication. The Beautiful and Damned (1922), The Great Gatsby (1925), Tender Is the Night (1934) and the unfinished The Last Tycoon followed, together with some 160 stories for the Saturday Evening Post. He died of a heart attack in Hollywood on 21 December 1940.
literary_profile: Fitzgerald is the essential novelist of the 1920s and the author of the most nearly perfect American novel: The Great Gatsby is a lyric study of the American dream's corruption, Tender Is the Night a study of money and marriage that is formally years ahead of its time, and the stories are the definitive record of the jazz age. His prose — the fresh, exact, romantic sentence — is the period's most influential style.
stylistic_characteristics: The romantic lyric sentence held in tight structure; the image chosen for its glamour and its hollowness; the collapse of the narrator's sympathy into judgement; the time-shift and the retrospective frame (Gatsby, Tender Is the Night); the short story built on a single social scene.
intellectual_concerns: The American dream and the corruption of it; money, class and the careless rich; the jazz age, drink and the party; love, marriage and the illusions of the beautiful; the Midwest and the East; failure, decline and the grace of the second chance refused.
historical_significance: Fitzgerald wrote the most perfect American novel of the period and the definitive record of the 1920s: The Great Gatsby is a permanent classic, Tender Is the Night is one of the century's great studies of marriage and money, and his short stories made the jazz age a literary period. He is the period's great poet of the American dream and its failure.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the hard-boiled sentence, the code hero and the modernist short story
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the revolutionary of American prose, the author of The Sun Also Rises and A Farewell to Arms, and the Nobel laureate of 1954.
biography: Born Ernest Miller Hemingway in Oak Park, Illinois, on 21 July 1899; he worked as a reporter on the Kansas City Star, served as an ambulance driver on the Italian front in 1918 and was badly wounded, and covered the Greco-Turkish war for the Toronto Star. Three Stories and Ten Poems (1923) and In Our Time (1925) made his name, The Sun Also Rises (1926) made him the voice of the Lost Generation, A Farewell to Arms (1929), For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940) and The Old Man and the Sea (1952) followed. He won the Nobel Prize in 1954 and died at Ketchum, Idaho, on 2 July 1961.
literary_profile: Hemingway changed the American sentence: his prose, built on the concrete noun, the plain verb and the omission of everything that can be left out, invented a style that the century has never escaped. In Our Time made the modernist short story an American form, The Sun Also Rises defined a generation, and A Farewell to Arms is the finest American novel of the First World War. The iceberg theory — that meaning lies in what is omitted — is his permanent contribution to narrative art.
stylistic_characteristics: The short declarative sentence; the concrete noun and the exact place-name; omission of the connective and the explanation; the dialogue that says less than it means; the repeated scene and the withheld emotion; the first-person narrator who does not comment.
intellectual_concerns: War, wounding and the code of endurance; the Lost Generation and the expatriate life; bullfighting, hunting and the mastery of fear; love and the loss of it; drink, Paris and the café; grace under pressure and the dignity of work.
historical_significance: Hemingway is the great revolutionary of American prose and the dominant American novelist of the period: his sentences changed how the century writes, In Our Time created the modern American short story, The Sun Also Rises and A Farewell to Arms are permanent, and the Nobel Prize confirmed his standing. He is the writer against whom every American stylist since has measured himself.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the collective novel, the newsreel collage and the documentary epic
literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the great experimental novelist of American social history and the author of U.S.A., the most ambitious American novel of the period.
biography: Born John Roderigo Dos Passos in Chicago on 14 January 1896; he read at Harvard, served in the Norton-Harjes ambulance corps and the American army in 1917–18, and published Three Soldiers (1921) and Manhattan Transfer (1925). The U.S.A. trilogy — The 42nd Parallel (1930), Nineteen Nineteen (1932) and The Big Money (1936) — was collected in 1938; he wrote over forty books of fiction, reportage and history, broke with the left after the Spanish Civil War, and died in Baltimore on 28 September 1970.
literary_profile: Dos Passos invented the collective novel: U.S.A. tells the history of America from 1900 to 1930 through twelve lives, interrupted by the Newsreel, the Camera Eye and the biographies of public figures — a technique of collage that gives the period its most complete social panorama. Manhattan Transfer is the first American novel of the modern city, and Three Soldiers one of the finest American novels of the war.
stylistic_characteristics: The collage of narrative, newspaper headline (Newsreel), autobiographical prose poem (Camera Eye) and biography; the discontinuous montage of lives; the flat documentary sentence; the panoramic city novel with no central protagonist; the slang and the song of the period transcribed.
intellectual_concerns: America as a collective social machine; the city and the crowd; labour, capital and the class war; the First World War and its profiteers; the lost generation and the political betrayal; the individual swallowed by history.
historical_significance: Dos Passos wrote the most ambitious American novel of the period: U.S.A. invented the collective documentary novel and gives the fullest social panorama of America 1900–1930, Manhattan Transfer created the modern city novel, and his collage technique influenced the political novel for the rest of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Southern Gothic, the mythical county and the novel of history's weight
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the greatest American novelist of the century, the creator of Yoknapatawpha County, and the Nobel laureate of 1949.
biography: Born William Cuthbert Falkner in New Albany, Mississippi, on 25 September 1897 and raised in Oxford, Mississippi; he served in the Canadian Royal Air Force in 1918 without seeing combat, worked briefly in New York and New Orleans, and published Soldiers' Pay (1926) and Mosquitoes (1927). Sartoris (1929), The Sound and the Fury (1929), As I Lay Dying (1930), Sanctuary (1931), Light in August (1932) and Absalom, Absalom! (1936) built the county of Yoknapatawpha; he worked in Hollywood, won the Nobel Prize in 1949 and the Pulitzer Prize twice, and died in Oxford, Mississippi, on 6 July 1962.
literary_profile: Faulkner is the greatest American novelist of the period: The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying and Absalom, Absalom! are among the most formally daring novels of the century, and the invention of Yoknapatawpha gave American literature a complete imaginative world to set beside Balzac's Paris or Hardy's Wessex. He made the burden of Southern history — slavery, defeat, guilt, the land — the matter of a great tragic art, and his late novels and stories extend the county to the edge of the modern world.
stylistic_characteristics: The long retrospective sentence with its parentheses and its piled-up subordinate clauses; the broken chronology and the multiple narrators; the interior monologue that renders illiteracy and idiocy; the Gothic grotesque and the violent scene; the county map and the family genealogy as apparatus; the rhetoric of the Southern pulpit.
intellectual_concerns: The Southern past and the burden of history; race, slavery and the guilt of the owning family; the family, the decaying house and the doomed line; the land and the wilderness; violence, sexuality and the honour code; endurance and the human capacity to prevail.
historical_significance: Faulkner is the greatest American novelist of the period and one of the great novelists of the century: The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying and Absalom, Absalom! changed the form of the novel, Yoknapatawpha is American literature's most complete imaginative world, and the Nobel speech is the period's most quoted statement of the writer's duty. He is the centre of the Southern Renaissance.
